authoredSolutions.1: For a particle of mass \(m\) with kinetic energy \(K\) the momentum is \(p=\sqrt{2mK}\), so \[\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}.\] Both particles carry the same \(K\), hence \[\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}=\frac{\sqrt{2m_{p}K}}{\sqrt{2m_{e}K}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{m_{e}}}.\] Since \(m_{p}\gg m_{e}\) the ratio exceeds 1, which is the expected result that the lighter electron has the longer wavelength.
authoredSolutions.2: With \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{0}\sin\omega t\) across a capacitor, \[i=\frac{dq}{dt}=C\frac{d\varepsilon}{dt}=\varepsilon_{0}\omega C\cos\omega t=\varepsilon_{0}\omega C\sin\left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right).\] The current therefore leads the emf by exactly \(90^{\circ}\), so on a phasor diagram the current phasor must sit a quarter turn ahead of the emf phasor. Option (A) draws \(\varepsilon\) along the horizontal axis and \(i\) along the vertical axis, a \(90^{\circ}\) lead, which is the pure capacitor. Option (B) shows \(i\) lagging by \(90^{\circ}\), which is a pure inductor, while options (C) and (D) show acute lead and lag angles, which correspond to RC and RL combinations rather than a bare capacitor.
authoredSolutions.3: Pure rolling gives \(v_{0}=\omega R\). For the rim point level with the centre the position vector from the centre is \(R\hat{i}\), so \[\vec{v}=v_{0}\hat{i}+\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r}=v_{0}\hat{i}+(-\omega\hat{k})\times(R\hat{i})=v_{0}\hat{i}-\omega R\hat{j}=v_{0}\hat{i}-v_{0}\hat{j}.\] Hence \[|\vec{v}|=\sqrt{v_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\,v_{0},\] so \(x=2\). The same follows from the instantaneous axis at the contact point, which is a distance \(\sqrt{2}R\) from that rim point, giving \(v=\omega\sqrt{2}R=\sqrt{2}v_{0}\).
authoredSolutions.4: Factor out \(\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}\): \[X=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}\left(\frac{A}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}\sin\omega t+\frac{B}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}\cos\omega t\right).\] Choosing \(\cos\phi=\frac{A}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}\) and \(\sin\phi=\frac{B}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}\) turns the bracket into \(\sin(\omega t+\phi)\), so \[C=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}},\qquad\tan\phi=\frac{B}{A}\Rightarrow\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{B}{A}\right).\] The amplitude is the vector sum \(\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}\), never the scalar sum \(A+B\), which rules out the third choice.
authoredSolutions.5: Intensity in terms of the magnetic amplitude is \[I=\frac{1}{2}\frac{cB_{0}^{2}}{\mu_{0}}\Rightarrow B_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{2\mu_{0}I}{c}}.\] Substituting \(I=0.92\ \text{W m}^{-2}\), \(\mu_{0}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T m A}^{-1}\) and \(c=3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), \[B_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{2(1.26\times10^{-6})(0.92)}{3\times10^{8}}}=\sqrt{7.71\times10^{-15}}=8.78\times10^{-8}\ \text{T}.\]
authoredSolutions.6: An infinite line charge produces \(E=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}x}=\frac{2k\lambda}{x}\) with \(k=9\times10^{9}\). With \(\lambda=4\times10^{-5}\ \text{C m}^{-1}\), \[E(10\ \text{mm})=\frac{2(9\times10^{9})(4\times10^{-5})}{1.0\times10^{-2}}=7.2\times10^{7}\ \text{V m}^{-1},\] \[E(12\ \text{mm})=\frac{7.2\times10^{5}}{1.2\times10^{-2}}=6.0\times10^{7}\ \text{V m}^{-1}.\] The field is non-uniform, so the two ends feel unequal forces. The negative end sits nearer the wire in the stronger field, giving a net attraction of magnitude \[F=q\left[E(10\ \text{mm})-E(12\ \text{mm})\right]=q\left(1.2\times10^{7}\right).\] Setting \(F=4\ \text{N}\), \[q=\frac{4}{1.2\times10^{7}}=3.3\times10^{-7}\ \text{C}=0.33\ \mu\text{C}.\]
authoredSolutions.7: If the plane of the dip circle makes an angle \(\alpha\) with the magnetic meridian, only the component \(B_{H}\cos\alpha\) of the horizontal field lies in that plane, while the vertical component \(B_{V}\) is unchanged. Therefore \[\tan\delta'=\frac{B_{V}}{B_{H}\cos\alpha}=\frac{\tan\delta}{\cos\alpha}.\] Because \(\cos\alpha\le1\) we get \(\tan\delta'\ge\tan\delta\), so the apparent dip always exceeds the true dip, \(\delta'>\delta\), with equality only when the circle is set in the meridian itself.
authoredSolutions.8: Place the semicircular wire of radius \(R\) in the upper half plane with its centre at the origin, as in the figure. An element subtending \(d\theta\) has mass \(dm=\frac{m}{\pi}d\theta\) and sits at \(y=R\sin\theta\), so \[y_{cm}=\frac{1}{m}\int_{0}^{\pi}R\sin\theta\cdot\frac{m}{\pi}\,d\theta=\frac{R}{\pi}\Big[-\cos\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi}=\frac{2R}{\pi}.\] Symmetry about the \(Y\) axis gives \(x_{cm}=0\). Comparing with \(\frac{xR}{\pi}\) yields \(x=2\).
authoredSolutions.9: For rolling without slipping down an incline, \[a=\frac{g\sin\theta}{1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}},\qquad t=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{a}}\propto\sqrt{1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}}.\] A ring has \(\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1\) and a solid cylinder has \(\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\), so \[\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+1}{1+\frac{1}{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}>1.\] The ring carries the larger moment of inertia for the same mass and radius, so more of the released energy goes into rotation, it accelerates less and \(t_{1}>t_{2}\).
authoredSolutions.10: Statement 1 is correct. Above the Curie temperature the thermal agitation overcomes the exchange interaction that aligns neighbouring dipoles, the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes and the material behaves as a paramagnet. Statement 2 is wrong. Heating does not increase the domains, it randomises the dipole orientations and breaks the domain structure down, so the net magnetisation falls rather than grows. Only statement 1 is true.
authoredSolutions.11: By the equipartition theorem each degree of freedom carries an average energy \(\frac{1}{2}kT\), so a molecule with \(f\) degrees of freedom has \(\overline{E}=\frac{f}{2}kT\). A monatomic molecule has only the three translational degrees of freedom, \(f=3\), hence \[\overline{E}=\frac{3}{2}kT.\]
authoredSolutions.12: Evaluate the two cross products. \[\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat{i}(1-0)-\hat{j}(1-0)+\hat{k}(1-0)=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k},\] \[\vec{B}\times\vec{C}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\0&1&1\\-1&1&0\end{vmatrix}=\hat{i}(0-1)-\hat{j}(0+1)+\hat{k}(0+1)=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}.\] Both have magnitude \(\sqrt{3}\), and their dot product is \(-1+1+1=1\), so \[\cos\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}\cdot\sqrt{3}}=\frac{1}{3}\Rightarrow\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right).\]
authoredSolutions.13: For line-of-sight transmission the radio horizon of a tower of height \(h\) is \(d=\sqrt{2hR_{e}}\), so \[h=\frac{d^{2}}{2R_{e}}.\] With \(d=1500\ \text{km}\) and \(R_{e}=6400\ \text{km}\), \[h=\frac{\left(1.5\times10^{6}\right)^{2}}{2\left(6.4\times10^{6}\right)}=\frac{2.25\times10^{12}}{1.28\times10^{7}}=1.76\times10^{5}\ \text{m}\approx175\ \text{km}.\]
authoredSolutions.14: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, so the angles of incidence and emergence are equal and \[\delta_{m}=i+e-A=2i-A\Rightarrow A=2i-\delta_{m}.\] With \(i=45^{\circ}\) and \(\delta_{m}=30^{\circ}\), \[A=2\left(45^{\circ}\right)-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}.\]
authoredSolutions.15: Newton's law of cooling makes the excess temperature over the surroundings decay exponentially, so equal time intervals multiply that excess by the same factor. In the first interval the excess falls from \(75-25=50^{\circ}\text{C}\) to \(65-25=40^{\circ}\text{C}\), a factor \(\frac{40}{50}=0.8\). Over the next equal interval the excess becomes \(40\times0.8=32^{\circ}\text{C}\), hence \[T=25+32=57^{\circ}\text{C}.\] The approximate average-temperature form agrees: \(\frac{10}{5}=k\left(\frac{75+65}{2}-25\right)=45k\) gives \(k=\frac{2}{45}\), and \(\frac{65-T}{5}=k\left(\frac{65+T}{2}-25\right)\) then yields \(T=57^{\circ}\text{C}\).
authoredSolutions.16: Clamping prevents the rail from expanding, so it is held at a thermal strain \[\text{strain}=\alpha\Delta T=\left(10^{-6}\right)(10)=10^{-5}.\] The stored elastic energy per unit volume is \[u=\frac{1}{2}Y(\text{strain})^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(10^{11}\right)\left(10^{-5}\right)^{2}=5\ \text{J m}^{-3}.\] Multiplying by the cross-sectional area gives the energy per unit length, \[\frac{U}{L}=uA=5\times0.01=5\times10^{-2}\ \text{J m}^{-1}.\]
authoredSolutions.17: Alpha decay of a nucleus with \(A=184\) leaves a daughter of mass number 180. The parent is at rest, so momentum conservation gives \(p_{\alpha}=p_{X}\) and \[\frac{K_{\alpha}}{K_{X}}=\frac{p^{2}/2m_{\alpha}}{p^{2}/2m_{X}}=\frac{m_{X}}{m_{\alpha}}=\frac{180}{4}.\] Since \(K_{\alpha}+K_{X}=Q\), \[K_{\alpha}=Q\,\frac{m_{X}}{m_{X}+m_{\alpha}}=5.5\times\frac{180}{184}=5.38\ \text{MeV}\approx5.4\ \text{MeV}.\] Almost all of the \(Q\) value goes to the light alpha particle, the heavy recoiling daughter taking only about \(0.12\ \text{MeV}\).
authoredSolutions.19: The scalar projection of \(\vec{A}\) on \(\vec{B}\) is \(\frac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{\left|\vec{B}\right|}\). Here \[\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=(1)(1)+(1)(1)+(0)(1)=2,\qquad\left|\vec{B}\right|=\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{3},\] so the projection is \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\).
authoredSolutions.20: The impulse on the bullet equals its change in momentum, \[J=m_{b}v_{b}=\left(4\times10^{-3}\right)(50)=0.2\ \text{kg m s}^{-1},\] which immediately rules out the two choices quoting \(200\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\). The gun and bullet start at rest, so momentum conservation gives \[M_{g}V=m_{b}v_{b}\Rightarrow V=\frac{0.2}{4}=0.05\ \text{m s}^{-1}=5\ \text{cm s}^{-1}.\] The impulse is therefore \(0.2\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and the recoil speed of the gun is \(5\ \text{cm s}^{-1}\).
authoredSolutions.21: Lowering at constant speed means \(\Delta KE=0\), so by the work-energy theorem the work of the external agent exactly cancels the work of gravity. As the body descends \(h=0.8\ \text{m}\), gravity does \[W_{g}=+mgh=(80)(10)(0.8)=+640\ \text{J},\] and therefore \[W_{ext}=-W_{g}=-640\ \text{J}.\] Equivalently, the external force is \(mg\) upward while the displacement is downward, so the two are antiparallel and \(W_{ext}=-mgh=-640\ \text{J}\).
authoredSolutions.23: Let the internal resistance be \(r\). With the \(5\ \Omega\) resistor the current is \(I_{1}=\frac{1.25}{5}=0.25\ \text{A}\), so \(E=1.25+0.25r\). With the \(2\ \Omega\) resistor the current is \(I_{2}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\ \text{A}\), so \(E=1+0.5r\). Equating the two expressions, \[1.25+0.25r=1+0.5r\Rightarrow0.25=0.25r\Rightarrow r=1\ \Omega.\] Hence \(E=1.25+0.25(1)=1.5\ \text{V}\), and from \(E=\frac{x}{10}\), \[x=10E=15.\]
authoredSolutions.44: Since \(\sin^7 x\le \sin^2 x\) and \(\cos^7 x\le \cos^2 x\) (as \(t^7\le t^2\) for \(t\in[0,1]\) and \(t^7<0\le t^2\) for \(t<0\)), \(\sin^7 x+\cos^7 x\le 1\), with equality only when \(\sin x,\cos x\in\{0,1\}\), i.e. \((\sin x,\cos x)=(1,0)\) or \((0,1)\). On \([0,4\pi]\): \(\cos x=1\) at \(0,2\pi,4\pi\) and \(\sin x=1\) at \(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{5\pi}{2}\), giving \(5\) solutions.
authoredSolutions.46: The numerator \(\cos^{-1}\sqrt{x^2-x+1}\) needs \(x^2-x\le0\Rightarrow x\in[0,1]\). The denominator \(\sqrt{\sin^{-1}(x-\tfrac12)}\) must be positive, so \(x>\tfrac12\). Intersection \((\tfrac12,1]\), giving \((\alpha,\beta)=(\tfrac12,1)\) and \(\alpha+\beta=\tfrac32\).
authoredSolutions.48: Using all five digits \(\{0,2,4,6,8\}\) without repetition gives \(5!=120\) strings; those with leading \(0\) number \(4!=24\). Every valid 5-digit number exceeds \(10000\), so the count is \(120-24=96\).
authoredSolutions.49: \(A\) swaps indices \(1,2\), so \(AB\) swaps rows \(1,2\) of \(B\) while \(BA\) swaps columns \(1,2\). Equating forces \(b_{11}=b_{22},\ b_{12}=b_{21},\ b_{13}=b_{23},\ b_{31}=b_{32}\), with \(b_{33}\) free: \(5\) independent entries, each from \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\), giving \(5^5=3125\).
authoredSolutions.52: Reading the linear terms as \(-108x+120y\), divide by \(36\): centre \(\big(\tfrac32,-\tfrac53\big)\) and \(r^2=\tfrac{9}{4}+\tfrac{25}{9}-\tfrac{C}{36}=\frac{181-C}{36}\). Not meeting either axis needs \(0<r<\min(\tfrac53,\tfrac32)=\tfrac32\), i.e. \(0<\frac{181-C}{36}<\tfrac94\Rightarrow 100<C<181\). So \(C\in(100,181)\).
authoredSolutions.53: An onto \(f:A\to A\) on a finite set is a bijection. Three distinct values summing to \(3\) must be \(\{0,1,2\}\), assigned to positions \(1,2,3\) in \(3!=6\) ways; the remaining \(7\) positions map bijectively to the remaining \(7\) values in \(7!=5040\) ways. Total \(6\cdot5040=30240\).
authoredSolutions.54: The line \(y=-2x+k\) is tangent to \(\frac{x^2}{3}-\frac{y^2}{3}=1\) when \(k^2=a^2m^2-b^2=12-3=9\Rightarrow k=\pm3\). Tangency to \(y^2=\alpha x\): substituting gives \(2y^2+\alpha y-\alpha k=0\) with discriminant \(0\Rightarrow \alpha=-8k\). Taking \(k=3\), \(\alpha=-24\).
authoredSolutions.56: For a die value \(r\), \(\omega^{r}\) depends on \(r\bmod 3\); each residue \(0,1,2\) occurs for two faces, probability \(\tfrac13\) each. Since \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\), the sum is \(0\) iff the three residues are a permutation of \(\{0,1,2\}\): probability \(3!\left(\tfrac13\right)^3=\frac{6}{27}=\frac29\).
authoredSolutions.57: Solve \((|x|-3)|x+4|=6\). For \(x\ge0\): \(x^2+x-18=0\Rightarrow x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{73}}{2}\) (one root). For \(-4\le x<0\): \(x^2+7x+18=0\) has negative discriminant (none). For \(x<-4\): \(x^2+7x+6=0\Rightarrow x=-1,-6\), only \(x=-6\) valid. Total \(2\) solutions.
authoredSolutions.59: The exponent is \(\frac{x}{\pi}-\big[\frac{x}{\pi}\big]\), so on \([n\pi,(n+1)\pi)\) with \(x=n\pi+t\) the integrand is \(\sin^2 t\,e^{-t/\pi}\), the same on all \(100\) intervals. With \(J=\int_0^{\pi}e^{-t/\pi}\sin^2 t\,dt=\frac{2\pi^3(1-e^{-1})}{1+4\pi^2}\), summing \(100\) copies gives \(I=\frac{200(1-e^{-1})\pi^3}{1+4\pi^2}\), so \(\alpha=200(1-e^{-1})\).
